subtopic_detail: Waist circumference rising by fourteen centimetres with a fasting glucose of 6.4 after ten months of olanzapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a twenty four year old man in a community clinic ten months after his first episode of psychosis. He has been taking olanzapine and his symptoms have remitted, and he has returned to a part time job.

He tells you he is sleeping well and is pleased with his progress, though his clothes no longer fit. He smokes ten cigarettes a day. He has no personal history of diabetes, and his father developed type 2 diabetes at fifty. He walks his dog most days but has stopped playing indoor soccer.

data_table.Examination: Weight 96 kg having been 78 kg at initiation, body mass index 30 kg/m2, waist circumference 104 cm having been 90 cm at initiation, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, no acanthosis nigricans, no tremor or rigidity, no abnormal involuntary movements
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glycated haemoglobin 42 mmol/mol (less than 42), total cholesterol 6.2 mmol/L (less than 5.5), triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein 0.9 mmol/L (greater than 1.0), liver function and full blood count within normal limits, prolactin 340 mIU/L (less than 400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and review his weight and metabolic profile again in twelve months time
options.rationale: An eighteen kilogram gain with impaired fasting glucose and dyslipidaemia represents established metabolic harm rather than a finding to observe, and a twelve month interval allows progression to frank diabetes. Metabolic monitoring is intended to trigger action rather than simply to document decline. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic entirely, since he has been in remission for most of the past ten months
options.rationale: Stopping treatment within the first one to two years after a first episode carries a high relapse rate, and each relapse is associated with poorer functional recovery. The metabolic problem is managed by changing the approach rather than by abandoning treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Discuss switching to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic burden, alongside lifestyle support and metformin
options.rationale: Olanzapine carries the highest weight gain and dyslipidaemia risk of the commonly used agents apart from clozapine, so switching to an agent such as aripiprazole is the intervention with the largest effect on this trajectory. Structured lifestyle intervention and metformin both have evidence for attenuating antipsychotic associated weight gain and are used alongside rather than instead of the switch. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose and add a low dose of quetiapine at night to maintain the overall antipsychotic effect
options.rationale: Combining two antipsychotics increases total adverse effect burden without evidence of better efficacy, and quetiapine carries its own appreciable metabolic risk. Polypharmacy would compound rather than resolve the problem. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Refer for bariatric surgery assessment given the weight gain and the developing impairment of glucose tolerance
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after sustained failure of medical and lifestyle measures, and the driving cause here has not yet been addressed at all. Operating before changing the medication responsible reverses the logical order of treatment. (Source: RACGP: Management of type 2 diabetes)

explanation.summary: People with schizophrenia die fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, and the excess is driven mainly by cardiovascular disease rather than by suicide, which makes metabolic monitoring a core part of psychiatric care rather than an optional extra. Australian practice recommends measuring weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or glycated haemoglobin and lipids at baseline, at six and twelve weeks, then at least annually, with more frequent review after any change. Antipsychotics differ substantially in risk, with clozapine and olanzapine at the high end, quetiapine and risperidone intermediate, and aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lurasidone at the lower end. When metabolic harm emerges the options are switching agent, adding metformin, and structured lifestyle intervention, and these are complementary rather than alternatives. Smoking cessation deserves separate attention because it compounds cardiovascular risk and because stopping raises clozapine and olanzapine levels through loss of cytochrome P450 1A2 induction.
key_points: Cardiovascular disease, not suicide, drives most of the excess mortality in schizophrenia
Monitor weight, waist, blood pressure, glucose and lipids at baseline, six and twelve weeks, then annually
Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest metabolic risk, aripiprazole among the lowest
Metformin and structured lifestyle intervention both attenuate antipsychotic associated weight gain
Antipsychotic polypharmacy increases adverse effects without demonstrated efficacy benefit
explanation.pearls: Stopping smoking removes cytochrome P450 1A2 induction and can raise clozapine and olanzapine concentrations by up to seventy per cent within a week, so a patient who quits needs dose review rather than congratulation alone.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Corrected calcium of 2.72 with a normal lithium level and stable mood after nine years of maintenance treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar conducting an annual review of a fifty three year old woman who has taken lithium for nine years for bipolar affective disorder. She has had no episode of mania or depression in seven years and works full time as a teacher.

She reports mild thirst but no polyuria, no tremor and no nausea. She takes no other regular medication and has not used non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. She reports some aching in her wrists and knees and general tiredness which she attributes to the school term.

data_table.Examination: Weight stable at 68 kg, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, fine physiological tremor only, no goitre, no dry skin or hair thinning, no proximal weakness, mood euthymic with normal speech and thought form
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L taken twelve hours post dose (0.6-0.8 maintenance), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90) and stable over five years, estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), corrected calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 8.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for endocrine assessment of hypercalcaemia while continuing lithium and monitoring the calcium
options.rationale: Lithium raises the set point at which the parathyroid glands sense calcium, producing a hyperparathyroid picture with a raised calcium and an inappropriately unsuppressed parathyroid hormone, and it explains her thirst, aching and fatigue. Endocrine assessment establishes whether this is lithium associated or a coincidental adenoma while treatment that has kept her well for seven years continues in the meantime. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose to achieve a level of 0.4 to 0.5 mmol/L and repeat the calcium in three months
options.rationale: The effect on parathyroid function is not clearly dose dependent, so reducing the dose is unlikely to correct the calcium while it does risk losing the prophylaxis that has kept her free of episodes. Lowering below the maintenance range increases relapse risk in bipolar disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and commence sodium valproate as a substitute mood stabilising agent for her
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of lithium carries a well described risk of rebound mania, and valproate is not an appropriate substitute chosen without discussion in a woman of this age with a strong lithium response. Any switch would be gradual and planned rather than immediate. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

options.text: Attribute the fatigue and aching to subclinical hypothyroidism and commence thyroxine replacement therapy now
options.rationale: Lithium does commonly cause hypothyroidism, which is why thyroid function is monitored, but the thyroid stimulating hormone here is squarely within the reference range. Treating a normal result would not address the abnormality that is actually present. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

options.text: Reassure her that these results are expected on long term lithium and repeat the full panel in twelve months
options.rationale: A raised calcium is indeed a recognised consequence of lithium, but recognising the mechanism is not a reason to leave persistent hypercalcaemia uninvestigated. Untreated hyperparathyroidism carries risks to bone density and renal stone formation over time. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long term treatment for bipolar affective disorder and the only agent with good evidence for reducing suicide, so the aim of monitoring is to keep people on it safely rather than to find reasons to stop. Australian monitoring includes serum lithium every three to six months once stable, taken twelve hours after the last dose, with renal function, thyroid function and calcium at least every six to twelve months. Three organ systems are affected in the long term. The thyroid is the commonest, with hypothyroidism in up to a quarter of patients, treated with thyroxine while lithium continues. The kidney may develop nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and, after many years, a slowly progressive interstitial nephropathy, while the parathyroid glands may develop a raised set point producing hypercalcaemia with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone.
key_points: Lithium is the only mood stabiliser with good evidence for reducing suicide risk
Monitor lithium level every three to six months with renal, thyroid and calcium testing at least annually
Levels are taken twelve hours after the last dose to be interpretable
Hypercalcaemia with unsuppressed parathyroid hormone reflects a raised parathyroid set point
Abrupt cessation risks rebound mania, so any change is gradual and planned
explanation.pearls: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, thiazide diuretics and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors all reduce lithium clearance and can precipitate toxicity within days, so a patient starting any of them needs a level checked within a week rather than at the next routine review.

sources.label: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Repeated relapse on patches alone in a heavy smoker with treated depression who wants the most effective option
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a forty seven year old woman who wants to stop smoking. She smokes twenty five cigarettes a day, lights her first within five minutes of waking, and has made four attempts in the past six years using nicotine patches alone, relapsing each time within a fortnight.

She has a history of recurrent depression, currently well controlled on sertraline for two years with no recent symptoms. She has no history of seizures, no cardiovascular disease and no renal impairment. She has read online that one of the tablets used for quitting causes psychiatric problems and asks you about this directly.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, chest clear on auscultation, no clubbing, mood euthymic with no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry shows a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted with a normal ratio, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Varenicline commenced one week before her chosen quit date, with review of mood at two and four weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the single most effective pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation and is the rational choice after repeated failure of single agent nicotine replacement in a heavily dependent smoker. The large randomised safety trial found no excess of serious neuropsychiatric events compared with patch or placebo, including in people with stable psychiatric illness, so her treated depression is a reason to monitor rather than to avoid it. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: Bupropion started two weeks before her quit date and continued for a total of nine weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Bupropion is an effective option but is less effective than varenicline in head to head comparison, and it interacts with serotonergic agents and lowers the seizure threshold. Choosing it ahead of varenicline accepts lower efficacy without a compensating safety advantage here. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: A higher strength nicotine patch used alone, with the dose increased in proportion to her daily cigarette count
options.rationale: Patch monotherapy is precisely the approach that has already failed her four times, and simply raising the strength does not address the breakthrough cravings that drive early relapse. Combination nicotine replacement adding a fast acting form would be the better way to use this class. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: Behavioural counselling through a telephone quit service alone, with no pharmacotherapy prescribed at this stage
options.rationale: Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates and should accompany any attempt, but withholding medication from a heavily dependent smoker with four failed attempts predicts another failure. Support and pharmacotherapy are complementary rather than alternatives. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: A nicotine vaping product obtained on prescription, used as the sole aid for the next three months of her attempt
options.rationale: Prescribed nicotine vaping is positioned in Australia as a second line option for people who have failed approved pharmacotherapies including varenicline, which she has not yet tried. Recommending it first bypasses the treatment with the strongest evidence. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

explanation.summary: Smoking remains the leading preventable cause of death in Australia, and every clinical contact is an opportunity to offer cessation support, which is most effective when behavioural support and pharmacotherapy are combined. Time to first cigarette is the single most useful measure of dependence, and smoking within thirty minutes of waking indicates high dependence that usually needs combination or more potent therapy. Varenicline has the strongest evidence of the available agents, followed by combination nicotine replacement pairing a patch with a fast acting form such as gum, lozenge, inhalator or mouth spray, then bupropion or single agent nicotine replacement. The historical concern that varenicline causes serious neuropsychiatric events was addressed by a large randomised trial which found no excess compared with patch or placebo, including in participants with stable psychiatric disorders, and the earlier boxed warning was subsequently removed. Relapse is expected and repeated attempts should be framed as normal rather than as failure.
key_points: Time to first cigarette is the most useful single measure of nicotine dependence
Varenicline has the strongest efficacy evidence, ahead of combination nicotine replacement
The large randomised safety trial found no excess neuropsychiatric events with varenicline
Combination nicotine replacement pairs a patch with a fast acting form for breakthrough cravings
Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates and is offered alongside any pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Smoking induces cytochrome P450 1A2, so quitting raises clozapine and olanzapine levels substantially within days and can also reduce caffeine clearance, which is one reason newly abstinent patients report jitteriness they attribute to withdrawal.

subtopic_detail: Request to conceive within a year while taking sodium valproate that has controlled mania for six years
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a twenty seven year old woman with bipolar affective disorder type one who has been stable on sodium valproate for six years, following two admissions with mania before that. She tells you she and her partner hope to start trying for a baby within the next twelve months.

She is currently euthymic, works as a physiotherapist and has good insight into her illness. She has never taken lithium. She uses no contraception at present and says she does not want to risk becoming unwell again, having been in hospital twice.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic features, speech normal in rate and volume, sleep seven to eight hours nightly, no suicidal ideation, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and renal function within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue valproate at the lowest effective dose and add high dose folic acid five milligrams daily before conception
options.rationale: Reducing the dose lowers but does not remove the risk, and folate supplementation has not been shown to prevent valproate associated malformation or neurodevelopmental harm. Treating a known teratogen as manageable with folate gives false reassurance. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Plan a switch to an alternative mood stabiliser with effective contraception maintained throughout the transition
options.rationale: Valproate carries roughly a ten per cent risk of major congenital malformation and a thirty to forty per cent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment, which makes it unsuitable in a woman planning pregnancy, and the time to plan a switch is before conception rather than after a positive test. Effective contraception is continued during the change because the transition period carries both teratogenic and relapse risk. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Stop valproate immediately without replacement and monitor her mood fortnightly until she becomes pregnant
options.rationale: Leaving a woman with two previous manic admissions unmedicated exposes her to a high relapse risk, and relapse in pregnancy or the postpartum period carries serious consequences for mother and infant. Cessation without a plan for continued prophylaxis trades one harm for another. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Continue valproate and arrange detailed foetal morphology ultrasound at eighteen weeks once she conceives
options.rationale: Morphology scanning detects some structural malformations but cannot detect the neurodevelopmental impairment that constitutes the larger part of the harm. Detection after the fact is not a substitute for avoiding the exposure. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Advise her to stop valproate as soon as she has a positive pregnancy test and review her urgently at that point
options.rationale: Neural tube closure is complete by about twenty eight days after conception, which is often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so stopping at a positive test occurs after the critical exposure window. It also risks abrupt destabilisation at the start of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic of the commonly used psychotropic medications, carrying a major congenital malformation rate of around ten per cent including neural tube defects, and a thirty to forty per cent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment encompassing lower cognitive scores and an increased rate of autism spectrum disorder. Australian regulators require that it not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, and then only with a pregnancy prevention programme including effective contraception and documented annual discussion of the risks. The key clinical point is that these conversations belong at every review of a woman of reproductive age rather than at the point a pregnancy is announced, because neural tube closure is complete before most pregnancies are recognised. Alternatives for bipolar prophylaxis in pregnancy include lithium, which carries a small absolute increase in cardiac malformation, and lamotrigine or quetiapine, which have more reassuring profiles. Withdrawal of all prophylaxis is rarely the right answer, since relapse risk rises sharply in pregnancy and particularly postpartum.
key_points: Valproate carries about a ten per cent malformation risk and thirty to forty per cent neurodevelopmental risk
Australian regulators require a pregnancy prevention programme for women of childbearing potential
Neural tube closure completes by about twenty eight days, before most pregnancies are recognised
Planning and switching happen before conception, not after a positive pregnancy test
Stopping prophylaxis altogether risks relapse, which is highest in the postpartum period
explanation.pearls: Postpartum psychosis affects around one in five women with bipolar affective disorder type one and typically declares itself within the first two weeks after birth, which is why a planned postnatal review in that window is written into the care plan before delivery.

sources.label: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate safety advisory

subtopic_detail: Escalating threats in an emergency department cubicle after verbal de-escalation and an offer of oral medication have failed
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a thirty two year old man brought in by police under the state mental health act after neighbours reported him shouting at passing cars. He is known to the service with schizophrenia and stopped his medication three months ago.

He is pacing his cubicle, shouting that staff are working for the people following him, and has punched the wall twice. Two nurses have spent twenty minutes attempting verbal de-escalation and have offered him oral olanzapine, food and a quiet space, all of which he has refused. He is now standing over a nurse with a clenched fist. A security team is present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Grazed knuckles with no deformity, pupils equal at 4 mm and reactive, no ataxia or nystagmus, no head injury reported by police, unable to complete cognitive assessment owing to agitation
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 6.1 mmol/L, point of care testing otherwise deferred owing to the level of agitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue verbal de-escalation without medication, since sedation should be avoided in an undifferentiated presentation
options.rationale: De-escalation has been properly attempted for twenty minutes and has failed, and continuing it while an assault is imminent places staff and the patient at risk. De-escalation remains first line but is not open ended when the situation is escalating. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Give intravenous midazolam in repeated increments until he is sufficiently settled for a full physical examination
options.rationale: Establishing intravenous access in a physically threatening patient is hazardous for staff, and intravenous benzodiazepine titrated to deep sedation carries a high risk of respiratory depression. The intramuscular route is preferred in this situation. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Give intramuscular droperidol with physical restraint only as long as needed, then continuous monitoring afterwards
options.rationale: When de-escalation and oral medication have failed and there is imminent risk of harm, parenteral sedation is indicated, and droperidol is the agent with the best Australian evidence for efficacy and safety in acute behavioural disturbance. Restraint is applied for the minimum time required to give the drug safely, and continuous observation with vital sign monitoring follows because sedation carries airway and cardiovascular risk. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Ask the police to remove him from the department and return him once he is calm enough to be assessed safely
options.rationale: He is detained under mental health legislation and presents with an untreated relapse of a psychotic illness, so the department owes him assessment and treatment. Discharging the problem to police abandons a duty of care. (Source: RANZCP: Acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Place him in mechanical restraints in a seclusion room and observe without giving any medication for four hours
options.rationale: Prolonged mechanical restraint without treatment does not address the underlying psychosis and carries risks including rhabdomyolysis, venous thromboembolism and positional asphyxia. Restraint is a bridge to treatment rather than a treatment in itself. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed along an escalating pathway that begins with environmental measures and verbal de-escalation, moves to offered oral medication, and reaches parenteral sedation only when those have failed and risk of harm is imminent. Reversible medical causes are actively considered throughout, since hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury, delirium and intoxication all present with agitation and are treated differently, which is why a capillary glucose is obtained even when full examination is impossible. Australian evidence, largely from emergency department randomised trials, supports droperidol as the first line parenteral agent, with midazolam or a combination used in some protocols and olanzapine as an alternative. Any patient who receives parenteral sedation requires continuous observation with regular vital signs, pulse oximetry and airway monitoring, because respiratory depression, hypotension and aspiration are the recognised harms. Restraint is used for the shortest time necessary, documented, and followed by debriefing with the patient once they are settled.
key_points: The pathway runs from environmental measures and de-escalation, to oral, then to parenteral medication
Reversible causes including hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury and intoxication are considered throughout
Droperidol has the best Australian emergency department evidence as a first line parenteral agent
Continuous observation with vital signs and pulse oximetry follows any parenteral sedation
Restraint is a bridge to treatment, applied for the shortest time and followed by debriefing
explanation.pearls: The corrected QT concern that historically limited droperidol arose from doses far above those used for acute behavioural disturbance, and Australian emergency trials of 10 mg intramuscularly found no clinically significant arrhythmia, which is why it regained first line status.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

subtopic_detail: QRS duration of 128 milliseconds three hours after an overdose taken with a rising drowsiness and a normal blood pressure
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a nineteen year old woman brought in by ambulance three hours after telling her flatmate she had swallowed a handful of her mother's tablets following a relationship breakdown. The flatmate has brought in an empty bottle labelled amitriptyline 50 mg.

She was drowsy but rousable on arrival and has become harder to wake over the last twenty minutes. She has taken no alcohol and no other medication. She has no history of cardiac disease and no previous overdose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 12, pupils dilated at 6 mm and sluggish, skin dry and flushed, bowel sounds reduced, no focal neurological deficit, bladder palpable
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 128 milliseconds and a prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR, venous pH 7.34 (7.32-7.42), bicarbonate 21 mmol/L (22-32), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), paracetamol level not detected, capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and prepare for intubation with ongoing electrocardiographic monitoring
options.rationale: A QRS above 100 milliseconds with a terminal R wave in aVR indicates sodium channel blockade and predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia, and hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote because it provides a sodium gradient and alkalinisation that displace the drug from the channel. It is given on the electrocardiographic finding rather than waiting for haemodynamic collapse, and the falling conscious state means the airway needs securing. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and improve her conscious state before further assessment
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which are not implicated here, and it is specifically contraindicated in mixed or tricyclic overdose because removing any benzodiazepine effect lowers the seizure threshold. It would raise rather than reduce the risk of convulsions. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

options.text: Give intravenous amiodarone to control the tachycardia and reduce the risk of progression to a ventricular rhythm
options.rationale: Class one and class three antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated in this poisoning. Treating the tachycardia as a primary arrhythmia misreads it as a consequence of the toxidrome. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal orally now and repeat the dose in four hours to reduce ongoing drug absorption
options.rationale: Charcoal is considered within about an hour of ingestion and requires a protected airway, so giving it orally to a patient with a falling conscious state at three hours risks aspiration for little benefit. Decontamination does not take priority over treating the cardiotoxicity. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

options.text: Observe with continuous cardiac monitoring and treat only if she develops seizures or a ventricular arrhythmia
options.rationale: The widened QRS is itself the marker that identifies who will deteriorate, and deterioration in this poisoning can be abrupt and difficult to reverse once established. Waiting for the complication forfeits the window in which the antidote works. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose remains a leading cause of death from deliberate self poisoning because toxicity involves several mechanisms at once and can progress rapidly. Sodium channel blockade slows cardiac conduction and produces the characteristic QRS widening, rightward axis shift and terminal R wave in lead aVR, and it predicts both seizures and ventricular arrhythmia. Anticholinergic effects give the dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention and reduced bowel sounds, while alpha blockade produces hypotension and central effects produce sedation and seizures. The electrocardiogram is the primary risk stratification tool, with a QRS above 100 milliseconds associated with seizures and above 160 milliseconds with ventricular arrhythmia, and serum drug levels are of no practical use. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the specific treatment, given for QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension, with intralipid emulsion considered in refractory cardiac arrest.
key_points: The electrocardiogram is the primary risk stratification tool and drug levels are not useful
QRS above 100 milliseconds predicts seizures and above 160 milliseconds predicts ventricular arrhythmia
A terminal R wave in lead aVR is the characteristic marker of sodium channel blockade
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote through sodium loading and alkalinisation
Flumazenil and class one or three antiarrhythmics are both contraindicated in this poisoning
explanation.pearls: Seizures in tricyclic overdose worsen the acidosis that increases free drug and deepen the sodium channel blockade, so they are terminated promptly with a benzodiazepine and followed immediately by further bicarbonate rather than by phenytoin, which shares the sodium channel effect.

subtopic_detail: Three days of mutism with waxy limb posturing and refusal of food in a woman with a long history of severe depression
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a fifty eight year old woman on a medical ward. She was admitted three days ago after her daughter found her sitting in a chair, not speaking and not eating, having withdrawn progressively over the preceding fortnight.

She has a twenty year history of recurrent severe depression with two previous admissions. She stopped her antidepressant four months ago. The medical team have completed a workup for an organic cause. She has taken no food or fluid orally for two days and has a peripheral cannula in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mute throughout, eyes open and tracking intermittently, limbs remain in positions in which they are placed for several minutes, resists passive eye opening, grasps the examiner's hand repeatedly when asked not to, no rigidity or tremor, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function and C reactive protein within normal limits, creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200), magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable, electroencephalogram shows generalised slowing with no epileptiform activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence an intravenous antibiotic for presumed encephalitis while awaiting cerebrospinal fluid analysis results
options.rationale: There is no fever, no raised inflammatory markers, no seizure activity and normal brain imaging, so an infective encephalitis is unlikely on the available evidence. Empirical antibiotics would delay a treatment that is both diagnostic and therapeutic here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Administer a lorazepam challenge and observe the response over the following ten to thirty minute period
options.rationale: Mutism with waxy flexibility, negativism and automatic obedience in a woman with severe depression describes catatonia, and a benzodiazepine challenge is both the diagnostic test and the first line treatment, with a partial or complete response within thirty minutes supporting the diagnosis. Recognising and treating it matters because untreated catatonia progresses to dehydration, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and the malignant form. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start an antipsychotic to treat the withdrawal and posturing as manifestations of an underlying psychotic depression
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate the malignant form of catatonia and are generally withheld until the catatonic syndrome has been treated. Psychotic depression may well be present, but the antipsychotic is added after rather than before the catatonia is addressed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Recommence her previous antidepressant at the dose she was taking before she stopped it four months ago
options.rationale: Antidepressants are part of treating the underlying depressive episode but take weeks to act and do not treat the catatonic syndrome. A woman who has taken nothing orally for two days needs an intervention that works within hours. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube for feeding and observe for a further seventy two hours before any psychiatric treatment
options.rationale: Nutritional support is an appropriate supportive measure but does not treat the syndrome causing the refusal to eat. A further three days of observation adds risk of thromboembolism and pressure injury without therapeutic benefit. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor dysregulation that occurs across mood disorders, psychotic illness and a range of medical and neurological conditions, and it is substantially underrecognised because clinicians expect it only in schizophrenia when in fact mood disorders are the commonest psychiatric cause. Its features include immobility, mutism, staring, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia and echopraxia, and standardised instruments such as the Bush Francis scale help to identify and quantify them. The benzodiazepine challenge serves as both diagnosis and treatment, with lorazepam producing a response in the majority within minutes to hours, and electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment for those who do not respond or who have the malignant form. Malignant catatonia adds fever, autonomic instability and rigidity with a raised creatine kinase, and is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is one reason antipsychotics are withheld. Untreated, the syndrome carries substantial mortality from dehydration, malnutrition, venous thromboembolism, aspiration and pressure injury.
key_points: Mood disorders, not schizophrenia, are the commonest psychiatric cause of catatonia
The benzodiazepine challenge is simultaneously the diagnostic test and the first line treatment
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive for non responders and for the malignant form
Antipsychotics may precipitate malignant catatonia and are withheld until the syndrome is treated
Untreated catatonia carries mortality from dehydration, thromboembolism and aspiration
explanation.pearls: Automatic obedience and mitgehen, where a limb moves with the lightest pressure like an anglepoise lamp, sit alongside waxy flexibility as bedside signs that take seconds to elicit and are far more specific than mutism or immobility alone.

subtopic_detail: Fever with lower limb clonus and hyperreflexia developing within eight hours of a dose increase and a new analgesic
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a forty one year old man brought in by his wife because he has become agitated, sweaty and shaky through the course of today. He has taken sertraline for two years and his general practitioner increased the dose four days ago.

Yesterday he saw a locum for back pain and was prescribed a new analgesic, which he started last night and has taken three doses of. His wife says he was completely well at breakfast and that the shaking began around lunchtime. He takes no other medication and does not use illicit drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and restless but oriented, pupils dilated at 6 mm, skin diaphoretic, sustained clonus at both ankles with hyperreflexia more marked in the legs than the arms, no lead pipe rigidity, tremor of both hands
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 640 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L, electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a normal QRS and corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous dantrolene and commence active cooling, treating this as a malignant hyperthermic reaction
options.rationale: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia from volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium and has no established role in this syndrome. The absence of an anaesthetic exposure and the pattern of neuromuscular findings point elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the offending agents, give intravenous benzodiazepines and fluids with active cooling and monitoring
options.rationale: Rapid onset within hours of adding a second serotonergic drug, with lower limb predominant clonus and hyperreflexia, hyperthermia and autonomic instability, describes serotonin toxicity, and treatment is withdrawal of the precipitants with benzodiazepines, fluids and cooling. Benzodiazepines reduce the muscular hyperactivity that generates the heat, which is what drives the rhabdomyolysis and the mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give intravenous bromocriptine and continue the sertraline, treating this as a neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine antagonist exposure, evolves over days rather than hours and produces lead pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia rather than clonus. He has taken no dopamine blocking drug, and continuing the serotonergic agent would prolong the toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and aciclovir after lumbar puncture, treating this as a central nervous infection
options.rationale: Meningoencephalitis is a reasonable differential for fever with altered mental state, but it does not produce lower limb predominant clonus with dilated pupils in a man who was well eight hours earlier. The clear temporal link to a drug change makes an infective cause unlikely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give a single dose of an antipsychotic for the agitation and continue observation on the short stay unit overnight
options.rationale: Antipsychotics with antidopaminergic and anticholinergic properties can impair heat dissipation and worsen the picture, and this patient needs more than overnight observation given his temperature and creatine kinase. Sedation with a benzodiazepine is the safer choice for agitation in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a predictable dose related consequence of excess serotonergic activity rather than an idiosyncratic reaction, and it most often follows the addition of a second serotonergic agent to an established one. The triad comprises neuromuscular excitation, autonomic instability and altered mental state, and the neuromuscular findings are the most discriminating because clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristically more pronounced in the lower limbs. The Hunter criteria formalise this, requiring a serotonergic agent plus spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or hypertonia with a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius and ocular or inducible clonus. Common Australian precipitants added to an antidepressant include tramadol, fentanyl, pethidine, linezolid, triptans, moclobemide and over the counter dextromethorphan. Treatment is supportive with removal of the precipitants, benzodiazepines, cooling and fluids, with cyproheptadine reserved for cases not responding and intubation with paralysis for severe hyperthermia.
key_points: Onset is within hours of a serotonergic drug change rather than over days
Clonus and hyperreflexia are more pronounced in the lower limbs and are the key discriminators
Tramadol added to an existing antidepressant is a common Australian precipitant
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives lead pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia and evolves over days
Treatment is cessation of precipitants with benzodiazepines, fluids and active cooling
explanation.pearls: A temperature above 41.1 degrees Celsius in serotonin toxicity is a critical threshold requiring immediate sedation, paralysis and intubation, because sustained muscular hyperactivity at that point produces rhabdomyolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi organ failure.

subtopic_detail: Longstanding inattention with exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death before the age of forty
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a developmental clinic reviewing a fourteen year old boy referred with longstanding inattention. Teacher and parent rating scales are concordant, symptoms have been present since early primary school across home and school, and a psychologist has documented impairment in two settings.

His mother mentions in passing that he fainted at football training twice this season, each time while running, and that he recovered within a minute. She adds that her brother died suddenly at thirty eight while jogging and that no cause was ever found. The boy sleeps well and there is no snoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Height and weight on the fiftieth centile, no murmur audible at rest, no abnormal precordial heave, peripheral pulses normal, no marfanoid features, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence methylphenidate at a low dose and monitor pulse and blood pressure at each subsequent clinic review
options.rationale: Routine cardiac screening before stimulants is not required for children with a normal history and examination, and this history is not normal. Exertional syncope with a family history of unexplained sudden death is exactly the situation in which the usual approach does not apply. (Source: RACGP: ADHD clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine instead of a stimulant, on the basis that it does not carry any cardiovascular risk
options.rationale: Atomoxetine also raises heart rate and blood pressure and carries its own cardiovascular cautions, so switching class does not remove the need to investigate. The problem is the undiagnosed cardiac risk rather than the specific drug chosen. (Source: RACGP: ADHD clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology with an electrocardiogram, deferring stimulant medication until assessed
options.rationale: Exertional syncope together with a first degree relative's unexplained sudden death before forty are red flags for inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy, and both warrant cardiology assessment regardless of any medication decision. Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure and are deferred until the cardiac risk has been characterised. (Source: RACGP: ADHD clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Arrange behavioural parent training and classroom accommodations, and review the syncope only if it recurs
options.rationale: Non pharmacological supports are valuable and should be arranged regardless, but treating the syncope as something to watch misses the point that exertional syncope may itself be the warning before sudden cardiac death. It requires investigation on its own merits. (Source: RACGP: ADHD clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Arrange a tilt table test to confirm vasovagal syncope before starting stimulant medication for his inattention
options.rationale: Syncope during exertion rather than on standing or after a trigger argues against a vasovagal mechanism, and a tilt table test would not exclude an inherited arrhythmia. It risks producing a falsely reassuring result. (Source: CSANZ: Guidelines for genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Guidelines for genetic heart disease

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is diagnosed on symptoms present before the age of twelve, occurring in two or more settings, causing functional impairment and not better explained by another condition, and stimulants remain the most effective treatment. Routine electrocardiography before starting a stimulant is not recommended in Australia for a child with an unremarkable cardiac history and examination, because the yield is low and the delays are real. That guidance rests entirely on a careful targeted history and examination, which is where red flags are meant to be caught. The specific red flags are exertional syncope or chest pain, palpitations with exertion, a known structural cardiac lesion, and a family history of sudden unexplained death, inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy in a relative under forty. Exertional syncope is never assumed to be vasovagal, since it is a presenting feature of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and anomalous coronary origin.
key_points: Diagnosis needs symptoms before age twelve, in two or more settings, with functional impairment
Routine electrocardiography before stimulants is not required when history and examination are normal
Exertional syncope and a relative's unexplained sudden death before forty are both red flags
Exertional syncope is never assumed to be vasovagal and requires cardiology assessment
Atomoxetine also raises heart rate and blood pressure, so switching class does not avoid the issue
explanation.pearls: Syncope occurring during exertion points to a structural or arrhythmic cause, whereas syncope immediately after stopping exercise is far more often vasovagal, and that single distinction in the history does more triage work than any bedside test.
